# Ezekiel 20:25–49: research notes

**Coverage:** I read Enduring Word (Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, Bible Hub's combined commentary pages for vv. 25, 37 and 47, StudyLight verse pages, bible.org (Utley) and Matthew Henry. I found nothing on these verses from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, any Lutheran site, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teacher, so those are left out. The pages don't name each writer's tradition. Where I give one in brackets, it's my own label, so please check it before you print it.

---

**v. 25: "statutes that were not good"**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik says Israel turned down God's law, so God let them live under the laws of other nations. He quotes Feinberg: "Disobedience leads to greater sin. Sin becomes its own punishment." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Ellicott says these can't be the life-giving laws of v. 11, so they aren't part of the law of Moses. These evil statutes and judgments were those adopted from the heathen. He compares Romans 1 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-25.htm
- Pulpit agrees. It says Ezekiel calls the darker kinds of idol worship "statutes" with grave irony, and that sin became, by God's appointment, the punishment of sin. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: abandoned them, and they abandoned themselves to the customs and ordinances of the heathen. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/ezekiel/20-25.html
- Chuck Smith's paraphrase of God's attitude: "All right, if that's what you want to do, do it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-26.html

*Where the traditions differ (this is the most debated verse in the passage)*
- **Calvin [Reformed]** says the "not good" laws are man-made inventions. People wear themselves out with them while thinking they are pleasing God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-25.html
- **Gill [Baptist]** offers several options. They might be the ceremonial laws, which were "not in their own nature good". They might be the punishments God sent. Or they might be heathen customs God allowed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-25.htm
- **Benson [Methodist]** mentions the ceremonial-law view but sides with Lowth: God "gave them up to a reprobate mind". — same URL
- **Keil & Delitzsch [Lutheran]** say it is perfectly self-evident that we are not to understand by these statutes and rights, which were not good, either the Mosaic commandments of the ceremonial law, as some of the Fathers and earlier Protestant commentators supposed. — same URL
- **Constable [dispensational]** gives the usual reading. He also adds that God did not lighten the burden of responsibility that the Mosaic Law imposed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-25.html

*Other views*
- **Catholic (Haydock):** God is often said to do what He only permits. Haydock calls the "abandoned them" reading the best one. He also records that early writers (Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome and others) saw the precepts as given in condescension to the weakness of the people, (Origen) particularly the ceremonial part. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-20.html
- **Cambridge Bible (older critical scholarship):** the law in view is passing firstborn children through the fire. It reads this evil law as a judicial punishment, like the "deception" of the false prophets. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-25.htm
- **Utley** notes the verse troubles many commentators because it seems to impugn God's character. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**v. 26: "unclean through their gifts"**
- Guzik: Israel honoured idols in terribly unclean ways, finally including child sacrifice. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Pulpit: "gifts" covers all God's blessings, including children. The resulting desolation would teach the people who the LORD really is. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Benson: God let them defile themselves by offering their firstborn to Moloch. This brought desolation, so that they would learn He is the true God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-25.htm
- Utley links this to the worship of Molech. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**vv. 27–28: idols on the hills**
- Guzik: Israel showed terrible ingratitude by using the very hills and trees God gave them for idol worship. Taylor calls taking over the Canaanite hilltop shrines "the crowning rebellion". — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Pulpit: it made the sin worse that it happened in the land God had sworn to give them. The "thick trees" point to Asherah worship. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm

**v. 29: "Bamah"**
- Pulpit: *bamah* first meant a hill where a local shrine stood, and later came to mean forbidden worship sites. Ezekiel mocks the word with a play on "go" + "what?". Pulpit also suggests "go in" carries a sexual hint, which fits the language of prostitution in v. 30. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Clarke paraphrases God: I called it במה bamah, to mark it with infamy; but ye continue to frequent it. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-20.html

**vv. 30–31: "Should I be consulted by you?"**
- Pulpit: the words are aimed first at the elders of v. 1, and through them at everyone in their generation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Guzik: *nothing had changed*. God owed no special revelation to such a disobedient people. Feinberg: the fathers' sins were mirrored in their children's lives. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Utley: the elders acted as if they wanted the LORD's advice, but in reality, they were idolaters. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**v. 32: "like the nations"**
- Utley (I can't tell from the page exactly which verse the note belongs to): Israel cannot be a light to the nations because she has become one of the nations! — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**v. 33: "I will rule over you"**
- Matthew Henry: rule he will, either with the golden sceptre or with the iron rod. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_020.cfm
- *Modern scholarship:* Guzik quotes a commentator who says that, read plainly, vv. 33–36 promise exiled Israel the opposite of salvation. The only "mercy" offered is to be confronted by its Master. (Guzik lists Vawter & Hoppe among his sources.) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/

**vv. 34–35: "the wilderness of the nations"**
- Guzik: God would restore Israel "with the same energy and intent" He used in scattering them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Pulpit: the prophecy looks beyond anything yet fulfilled. The return under Zerubbabel was only a pledge of it. The "wilderness of the peoples" may be the Syro-Arabian desert. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Keil (a contrasting view): this bringing-out is an act of God's anger. It can't simply mean the return from Babylon or a future regathering. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-37.htm

**v. 36**
- Bible Hub's chapter study says the regathering involves judgment "in the wilderness of the peoples", like the wilderness after Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/20.htm

**v. 37: "pass under the rod … bond of the covenant"**
- Most writers see a shepherd counting his sheep (Lev 27:32): Ellicott, Barnes, JFB and Utley. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-37.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20
- Clarke ties it to tithing sheep: the shepherd marked every tenth animal with a rod dipped in vermilion. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-37.html
- Guzik: the exile would correct Israel, and the covenant would be restored. — https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Eze/Eze-20.cfm

*Where the traditions differ*
- **Calvin [Reformed]** reads it as a warning. God will call apostates to account. He holds them by the covenant not to rule over them as a father, but to punish their revolt more severely. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-37.html
- **Gill [Baptist]** applies it to the converted Jews in the latter day. The "bond" is the discipline God provides within the covenant. — same URL
- **Keil [Lutheran]** says the "bond" includes the covenant's promises as well as its threats. Both are bonds God uses to train His people. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-37.htm
- **Chuck Smith** puts it in the future: God will make Israel pass under the rod and enter the covenant. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-37.html
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon applies it to grace. God brings His people out from under the law and place them under the covenant of grace. — https://biblehub.com/sermons/ezekiel/20-37.htm

*Other views*
- Cambridge Bible: the word "bond" isn't found anywhere else. The Greek may read "by number", and "covenant" may be a copying duplicate of the next word, "purge". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-37.htm

**v. 38: purging the rebels**
- Guzik: not everyone in exile would return. The purging itself would reveal who the LORD is. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Matthew Henry: there will come a distinguishing day, when God will separate between the precious and the vile. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_020.cfm

**v. 39: "Go and serve your idols"**
- Guzik: it's a stark choice. Serve your idols fully, or commit to God fully. Divided worship profanes His name. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Barnes calls it Strong irony. He notes another rendering that turns the verse into a promise that they will listen later. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/ezekiel/20-37.html

**v. 40: "My holy mountain"**
- Pulpit: Ezekiel sees Israel finally worthy of its name, with idols rooted out. "All of them" points to the end of the split between Israel and Judah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Bible Hub's study links this to the messianic kingdom of chs. 40–48 and Revelation 20–22. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/20.htm

**v. 41: "a pleasing aroma"**
- Guzik: bringing them back would be like a pleasing sacrifice, and it would glorify God before the nations. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Utley: this is a priestly phrase showing God accepts the returned remnant. Ezekiel was himself a trained priest. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**v. 42: "into the land of Israel"** (the views differ here)
- Guzik [listed under Pentecostal/charismatic in your brief]: this was true of the return from the Babylonian exile; it was also true of Israel's 1948 return to the land. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Gill (see v. 37) puts the fulfilment in the conversion of the Jews in the latter days. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-37.html
- Bible Hub's chapter outline sums up v. 33 onward as: He promises to gather them by the Gospel. — https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/20-25.htm

**v. 43: "you will loathe yourselves"**
- Pulpit: the evil past is still remembered after forgiveness, and the humility that comes from that memory protects the new blessedness. Pulpit even suggests eternal shame could exist alongside eternal life. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: The more conversant we are with God's holiness the more we shall see of the odious nature of sin. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_020.cfm

**v. 44: "for the sake of My name"**
- Bible Hub: the phrase appears four times in the chapter (vv. 9, 14, 22, 44). — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/20.htm
- Utley: the principle "we reap what we sow" is abrogated by the mercy and eternal redemptive purposes of YHWH. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**vv. 45–46: "set your face toward the south"**
- Guzik: "the south" means Judah, south of Ezekiel in Babylon. He quotes a note that the Hebrew for "preach" is literally closer to "spit". — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- Pulpit: "drop thy word" is a term for prophetic speech. Three different Hebrew words are used for "south". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/20.htm
- Utley: all these names point to Jerusalem (cf. 21:1). — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-20

**v. 47: green tree and dry**
- Guzik: the fire is the Babylonian army. It burns both the plainly guilty and the relatively righteous. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/
- JFB and Keil read green and dry as the righteous and the wicked (cf. 21:3–4). Ellicott thinks Jesus may have had this in mind in Luke 23:31. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/20-47.htm ; https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/20-47.htm
- Clarke gives a social reading: the green trees are the most important people and the dry trees the lowest. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/20-47.html
- Gill says the righteous and the wicked suffer the same earthly disasters, but they shall not perish everlastingly together. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-21.html

**v. 48**
- Bible Hub's study says the unquenchable fire signals that nobody escapes. — https://biblehub.com/study/ezekiel/20-47.htm

**v. 49: "just telling parables"**
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: an unwilling heart finds any message from God hard to understand. — https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-20.cfm
- Bible Hub: the listeners miss that the warning is meant literally. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/20.htm

---

**Gaps:** I found no Orthodox, Lutheran-site, Pentecostal-denomination (ag.org) or Wesley's Notes material on these verses. I also found no netbible.org notes and no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. Verses 30–32, 36 and 48 have thin coverage. I ran out of searches, so a second round on netbible.org, Wesley's Notes and Calvin's notes on vv. 39–44 would help.
